mech: The Arab conquests split the Mediterranean, cutting Gaul off from eastern papyrus, spices and gold, so the Frankish West turned inland.
Pottery and shipwreck counts fall from the 6th century as the Roman tax-and-army system that had moved bulk goods dissolved, a century before the Arabs arrived.
Repeated plague waves from 541 thinned the port populations and crews that had carried bulk trade.
Abbasid silver moving up the Russian rivers into the Baltic quickened the North Sea emporia, Dorestad and Hedeby among them, that traded with the Franks.
Captives sold from Europe through Venice and Verdun to the caliphate paid for the silver, spices and silks that drove the late-8th-century upturn.
With the sea closed, power moved north to the Austrasian Franks, landed lords with no Mediterranean outlet: without Muhammad, Charlemagne would be inconceivable.
The shipping lanes, fairs and coinage rebuilt c.775-900 were the platform that Venetian and later Genoese merchants scaled up.
Fatimid Egypt's huge internal flax-and-linen economy, visible in the Cairo Geniza letters, generated the Mediterranean demand that Italian ships later tapped.
Merchant settlements beside castles and bishoprics grew into towns whose burghers bought or fought for self-government.
Long-distance trade spread wealth to new families and opened Venetian institutions; the richest then used it to close the Great Council in 1297 and monopolise the state galleys.

view: van Zanden, Buringh & Bosker; David Stasavage
mech: Rulers who needed town money had to summon assemblies; by 1300 parliaments with power over taxes met across Latin Europe.
As the last Carolingian counts' public courts dissolved, castellans with mounted followers took over justice and imposed new "bad customs" on peasants.
Lordly violence was there before 1000 too; what changed was the record, as charters replaced court proceedings, so the "revolution" is largely an artefact of the sources.
The year 1000 ended ancient slavery and set up the seigneurie: lords skimmed surplus from newly free peasant families and spent it in markets, which started growth.
A surplus of younger sons trained as armoured horsemen and castle-builders exported the lordship model to Ireland, Iberia, the Baltic and the Levant.
Lords who supplied heavy cavalry could bargain with kings; European rulers came to outlast Muslim sultans, who relied on slave soldiers and faced no landed aristocracy.
The same knightly surplus and papal reform that pushed into Spain and the Slav lands answered Urban II's call in 1095.
Warm, settled summers c.950-1250 let farming climb uphill and north while Europe's population roughly doubled.
Markets, money and towns let more people live by specialising and trading food from surplus regions.
The 1257 Samalas eruption, the largest of the millennium, loaded the stratosphere with sulphate and helped tip the climate out of its medieval regime.
The shift into a cooler, stormier regime brought the torrential rains of 1314-16 that rotted grain in the fields across northern Europe for two or three years running.
With holdings subdivided and poor soils under the plough, millions lived so close to subsistence that bad harvests became mass death.
Scottish raids after Bannockburn and royal purveyance for war stripped northern England and Flanders of grain and stock just as harvests failed.
Herds already short of fodder after the wet years met a cattle plague, probably rinderpest, that killed most of the oxen and cows where it struck.
Losing draught oxen cut ploughing and manure for years and left tenants unable to pay, hitting manorial accounts before the plague.
Children who survived the famine and the loss of milk cows grew into frailer adults; London skeletons show the frail were likelier to die of plague in 1348-49.
Young, displaced rural poor of the famine years filled the shepherds' bands, which turned on royal officials and Jewish communities.
Perhaps 5 to 10 percent of northern Europeans died in 1315-17 and population growth stopped; arrears and vacant holdings began to pile up on manors.
Wet-then-dry swings in Central Asian climate collapsed gerbil colonies and pushed infected fleas onto caravans; tree-ring signals precede European plague outbreaks by about 15 years.
Overpopulation and exhausted soils had already ended growth; the plague arrived as the Malthusian check on a population that had outrun its land.
The plague hit every node of the Flanders-to-China trade circuit at once and, with Mongol power collapsing, the linked system came apart: the fall of the East came before the rise of the West.
The vacuum left in Indian Ocean and Asian trade after 1350 let a peripheral Europe later push into networks it had once joined as a junior partner.
Killing perhaps 40 to 60 percent of Europeans cut the labour supply; English farm workers' real wages roughly doubled between the 1340s and the mid-15th century.
Landlords in Parliament answered the labour shortage by trying to freeze wages at pre-plague levels and force the idle to serve.
Thirty years of prosecutions under the labour laws, then the poll taxes of 1377-81, turned rising peasant expectations into revolt.
Survivors knew their labour was worth more; Cohn finds revolts after 1348 aimed more often at liberty and political voice than at bread.
After Poitiers (1356) captured King John, nobles who had failed to defend the country demanded ransom money while companies of soldiers plundered the countryside.
Plague-thinned villages and lords squeezing scarcer tenants added to the anger behind the 1358 rising.
Florentine wool workers, scarcer after repeated plagues, demanded their own guilds and a share of government.
The rising showed lords the limits of coercion; labour services and bond tenures faded over the next century.
With land plentiful and tenants scarce, lords bargained: leases and money rents replaced labour services, and English serfdom was largely gone by the early 15th century.
Where land was abundant and labour scarce, free peasants, free land and non-working lords cannot coexist; east of the Elbe, with weak towns and strong noble diets, lords chose to tie peasants down.
Growing western cities paid well for Baltic grain, so Polish and Prussian lords turned to demesne farming for export with forced labour.
Serf demesnes producing grain for Amsterdam kept eastern Europe a raw-material periphery with weak towns and low productivity.
English peasants won freedom but not secure tenure; lords consolidated land into big leases for tenants who had to compete, improve and hire wage labour.
French peasants won near-freehold tenure, backed by a monarchy that wanted them as taxpayers; tiny holdings blocked consolidation and productivity stalled.
With fewer mouths, grain prices sagged while wool held up; lords turned shrunken arable villages into enclosed sheep runs.
Enclosure and engrossing swept away customary tenants and created the large consolidated farms of the new system.
Market-dependent tenant farmers raised output per worker, releasing labour to industry and building a home market.
Fewer tenants and falling grain prices after the 1370s squeezed rents; seigneurial income in eastern Normandy collapsed.
note: Feeds a process already under way, so contributed_to rather than caused.

mech: The falling rate of the feudal levy on ever-smaller holdings had started the crisis by c.1315, before the plague.
Nobles short of rent sought income from war, ransom and royal wages, feeding the Anglo-French wars.
Post-plague land abundance favoured pastoral farming, where women's labour was valuable; working as servants for years, they married later and had fewer children.
Late, consensual marriage and female wage work in the North Sea region built skills and held fertility below the Malthusian maximum.
The pattern was most extreme in places that did not grow, such as Germany and Scandinavia, so it cannot by itself explain the North Sea's rise.
Survivors had more income per head and spent it on town goods; cities and wars, both deadly, kept death rates high, which locked in high incomes.
Urban demand, trade and specialisation compounded where cities grew fastest, in the Low Countries and England.
The shock hit all of Europe alike; outcomes diverged because North Sea institutions (strong towns, parliaments, flexible labour markets) let high wages persist while elsewhere they were clawed back.
As numbers recovered after 1470, real wages across most of Europe sank back toward pre-plague levels by 1600; only London and Amsterdam held on.
Egypt's absentee Mamluk lords squeezed the survivors harder and let the irrigation works decay, so output fell for 150 years instead of recovering.
Plague made skilled labour, copyists included, dear, rewarding a labour-saving way to reproduce books.
Christians read the plague as divine punishment and some sought to appease God by public self-scourging; Muslim communities, as Dols shows, answered with prayer and processions but no flagellants.
Accusations of well-poisoning spread from Savoy up the Rhine in 1348-49; whole communities were burned, often before the plague itself arrived.
Across 1100-1800, colder growing seasons raised the chance of attacks on Jews, especially where rulers were weak.
Labour shortage and flooded workings cut mine output while Europe kept paying silver to the Levant for spices, draining coin.
High silver prices made it worth draining deep mines and using the new liquation process in Saxony, Bohemia and Tyrol.
Central European silver output multiplied several times between 1460 and 1530, and prices had begun to rise before American treasure arrived in bulk.
Egypt's failure to recover from the same shock that freed English labour is an early fork between the Middle East and north-western Europe.
American treasure registered at Seville rose to a peak in the 1590s, and Andalusian prices rose roughly fourfold over the century in step with it.
Population grew faster than food output, so grain prices rose more than other prices, and urbanisation sped up the circulation of money.
Demand-driven inflation outran wages for a century; falling real incomes, rising rents and state deficits broke in the crisis of the 1620s-1650s.
Ming taxes payable in silver made silver worth about twice as much in gold in China as in Europe, so it paid to ship Andean silver across the Pacific.
Mercury amalgamation multiplied Potosí's output after 1572; a large share went west from Acapulco to Manila.
Silver flowed until its value in China fell to the European level; the price revolution ended in the 1640s as the arbitrage closed.
Cheap European silver flowed east through the Levant trade, raising Ottoman prices against fixed salaries and tempting the treasury to debase.
Paying more musket infantry in cash during the 1578-90 war with Iran pushed the treasury to cut the akçe's silver content by close to half in 1585-86.
Debasement cut the real pay of janissaries and provincial cavalry; the 1589 janissary revolt and, later, discharged musketeers turned bandit followed.
Silver inflows raised the prices of non-traded goods and wages relative to tradables, so Castilian textiles lost out to imports: a 16th-century Dutch disease.
Silver remittances were the collateral that let Philip II borrow far ahead of revenue; when fleets were late or wars ran on, he rescheduled, and bankers still profited.
The 1575 suspension of payments left the Army of Flanders unpaid; mutineers sacked Antwerp in November 1576.
The fall of Antwerp and the closing of the Scheldt pushed merchants, capital and skilled Protestants to Amsterdam, which took over the "rich trades".
A century of inflation and land sales shifted wealth from crown and old nobility to the gentry, who then demanded a political voice to match.
Printers trained in Mainz carried the method down the Rhine and over the Alps; by 1500 presses had worked in more than 200 towns.
note: Feeds a process already under way, so contributed_to rather than caused.

mech: Cities that adopted printing in the 1400s grew markedly faster in the 1500s than similar cities that did not, using distance from Mainz to rule out reverse causation.
Towns with a press by 1500 were markedly more likely to turn Protestant by 1530 and 1600, a result that survives instrumenting with distance from Mainz.
Print fixed and multiplied texts; a vernacular Bible and identical tracts in thousands of hands made a heresy unsuppressible for the first time.
Print made the Renaissance permanent: classical texts could no longer be lost, and errata lists turned scholarship into cumulative correction.
Standardised tables, maps and diagrams let scholars compare and correct, the precondition of the scientific revolution and the Republic of Letters.
Early print was full of piracy and error; credibility had to be built by licensers, stationers and learned societies, so print's effects were made, not inherent.
Luther switched to short, cheap German tracts that Wittenberg printers could turn round in days, and his writings dominated German presses for a decade.
Printed polemic reached every literate town in German lands within weeks, making Luther's case a public movement before Rome could respond.
Woodcut broadsheets and sermons read aloud carried "godly law" into villages where few could read; the Twelve Articles of 1525 ran through about two dozen printings in weeks.
Peasants turned the reformers' appeal to scripture against tithes and serfdom: if Christ freed all, bondage was unchristian.
With Habsburg armies tied down by the Ottomans in Hungary and at Vienna, Charles V had to concede to the Lutheran princes; Ottoman pressure correlates with fewer intra-Christian wars.
Protestant rulers seized church property; graduates switched from theology to secular careers and building moved from churches to palaces and offices.
Luther urged every Christian to read scripture; in 19th-century Prussia Protestant counties were more literate, which explains most of their higher incomes.
Cities that adopted Protestant church ordinances set up schools and poor relief and attracted more upper-tail talent, then grew faster.
Calvinist worldly asceticism made disciplined work and reinvestment a sign of grace, the spirit of capitalism.
Protestant and Catholic towns in the German lands grew at the same rate from 1300 to 1900: no Weber effect shows up.
The loss of saints' days and later of "Saint Monday" lengthened the English work year; Voth estimates annual hours rose about a fifth between 1760 and 1830.
Sultans who drew legitimacy from the religious establishment had little reason to allow a technology that would undercut it.
Islamic learning was authenticated person to person, teacher to student; print threatened that chain, so scholars did not ask for it.
Without the press, the Ottoman lands missed cheap information, and rulers never had to shift their legitimacy from clerics toward economic elites.
French siege guns knocked down tall medieval walls in Italy in 1494-95; engineers answered with low, thick, angled bastions.
Bastioned towns could only be starved out by long sieges, so armies grew several-fold between 1500 and 1700.
Volley fire by countermarch and Swedish linear tactics needed drilled, permanent soldiers, so standing armies paid by states.
Swedish linear formations and light field guns beat Tilly's deep tercios at Breitenfeld in 1631.
Infantry victories such as Crécy and then the French siege train that retook Normandy and Gascony by 1453 were earlier, sharper revolutions: change came in bursts.
The decisive growth of armies and administration came after 1660, under Louis XIV and his rivals, and was built by bargaining with elites rather than by technology.
War made states: rulers who could tap capital or coerce out-fought the rest; some 500 European political units in 1500 fell to about 25 by 1900.
Once wars became expensive, money decided them; states with weak fiscal capacity lost or were absorbed, and the survivors built tax systems.
Countries that had to mobilise domestic resources for land war (Brandenburg-Prussia, France) dismantled their medieval estates; those shielded by water or allies (England, the Dutch) kept them.
After 1688 Parliament controlled taxes and guaranteed debt, so Britain could tax heavily and borrow cheaply to fight France.
A parliament able to veto the crown made default costly, so lenders accepted lower interest and the state could borrow far more.
Constant war among similar-sized states with cheap access to capital pushed Europeans furthest down the learning curve in gunpowder technology.
Europe's edge was small before c.1750: Ming and Qing forces matched European guns, and Zheng Chenggong drove the Dutch from Taiwan in 1662.
In the Americas epidemics and native allies did more than guns; in Asia and Africa Europeans stayed coastal supplicants until the late 18th century.
Atlantic sailing ships carrying broadside guns could dominate sea lanes that galleys and Asian merchantmen could not contest.
Trade followed the flag: armed trade and plantation conquest created Atlantic commerce, and wars decided who got it.
Military power secured markets, raw materials and shipping, which fed back into the wealth that paid for more power.
Compass, chart and the ocean-going ship made regular Atlantic crossings possible.
Plague, typhus and famine following the armies killed far more than battle; Wilson puts the Empire's loss near 20 percent, older estimates a third.
The Bohemian estates' revolt against Ferdinand of Styria drew in the Palatinate, Spain, Bavaria and, in time, Denmark, Sweden and France.
Religion mattered because it was built into disputes over the Empire's constitution; Wilson rejects calling it primarily a war of religion.
The 1648 settlement entrenched three legal confessions in the Empire and protected minorities by law.
The 1640s were among the coldest decades of the millennium; shortened growing seasons and drought or deluge ruined harvests from Ireland to China.
Low solar activity from 1645 coincided with frequent volcanic eruptions and El Niño episodes, deepening the cold.
A fatal synergy: climate shocks hit states already stretched by war and debt, and revolts, wars and famines clustered worldwide in the mid-century.
European temperature series show year-to-year noise, not a lasting shift; crises blamed on the Little Ice Age are bad years picked after the fact.
Proxy reconstructions show the coldest century of the Little Ice Age came at different times in different regions, so a single global cold pulse cannot explain a worldwide crisis.
The crisis shook out the Mediterranean and central European economies and concentrated trade, capital and manufacturing on the North Sea, where growth continued.
Swollen Renaissance courts consumed the revenue of the "country"; the revolts of the 1640s were the country turning on the court.
Three kingdoms with three religions under one king: Charles I's prayer book for Scotland in 1637 set off the chain of wars.
Population growth since 1500 inflated prices, crowded elite competition for office and starved the crown's fixed revenues until the state broke.
The same demographic-structural squeeze (more people, dearer food, more elite aspirants, a fixed tax base) broke Ming China as well as Stuart England.
By 1600 population had refilled the land; subdivided holdings and falling real wages left millions exposed to the shocks of the 1620s-1640s.
The 1647-52 harvest failures pushed Paris bread to famine prices just as war taxes provoked the Parlement.
War with Spain, which continued after 1648, forced new fiscal edicts that the Paris Parlement refused to register.
The wettest summers in memory and harvest failures in 1646-50 deepened radical protest and the army's politics.
In 1647 bad harvests and a new tax on fruit, the poor's summer food, set off Masaniello's revolt in Naples and a rising in Palermo.
Olivares's demands that Catalonia and Portugal pay and quarter troops for the war with France set off revolts in 1640.
Hobbes wrote in Paris exile during the civil wars; his war of every man against every man was the world he watched, and his cure was an undivided sovereign.
Cooling weakened the summer monsoon, bringing north China's worst drought in centuries in 1637-41.
Drought, locusts and famine swelled the rebel armies of Li Zicheng, who took Beijing in 1644.
Epidemics of the 1630s and 1640s killed huge numbers in north China and the capital on the eve of the fall.
The more Ming taxes depended on imported silver, the more a supply shock from Manila and Nagasaki could squeeze taxpayers.
A fall in silver imports raised the real burden of silver taxes in the 1630s, adding to rural distress.
Silver imports did not fall sharply until after the dynasty was already collapsing; the Ming fell for fiscal and military reasons of its own.
Cold brought easterly winds that sped Dutch fleets, frozen canals for sledges and Baltic grain shortages the Dutch could profit from; the Republic turned climate stress into advantage.
The 1600 Peruvian eruption helped make 1601 one of the coldest summers in six centuries; Russian crops failed three years running.
Famine discredited Tsar Boris Godunov, filled the south with desperate fugitives and Cossacks, and opened the way to pretenders.
note: Feeds a process already under way, so contributed_to rather than caused.

mech: The late 16th century saw cold springs and wet, cool summers in central Europe, with frequent failed harvests and vintages.
Hail, frosts and failed vintages were blamed on weather-making witches; trial waves follow the worst years.
Across European regions, colder decades saw more witchcraft trials: witches were scapegoats for economic shocks.
The coldest decade in centuries, with drought in Anatolia, came on top of requisitions for the Long War; famine pushed peasants into the celali bands.
The "great flight" emptied villages; registers show many rural settlements abandoned and herders moving onto former farmland.
A cold, wet 1692 growing season ruined French grain; the famine of 1693-94 killed well over a million people.
Frosts in 1695-97 destroyed Finnish harvests; perhaps a quarter to a third of the population died.
Cooling and spreading sea ice after c.1300 shortened the hay season and cut the sailings to Norway.
The 1629-31 plague killed around 30 to 35 percent of northern Italy's people, a far heavier blow than plagues in England or the Netherlands, just as rivals rose.
The 1656 plague killed about half of Naples and much of the south, compounding the north's losses.
Europe's richest region in 1500 fell behind the North Sea economies, shifting the continent's centre of gravity.
Where monarchy was already checked, as in England and the Netherlands, Atlantic profits enriched merchants outside royal control, who fought for stronger property rights.
Atlantic merchants were a core of the parliamentary side in the 1640s and of the 1688 settlement.
Almost all of western Europe's extra growth from 1500 to 1850 came from Atlantic-trading nations and above all their Atlantic ports.
Profits of the slave trade and Caribbean sugar financed British industry, and Atlantic markets built on enslaved labour absorbed a large share of new cotton and metal goods.
Slave-trade profits were too small relative to domestic investment to drive industrialisation; the periphery was peripheral.
Enslaved Africans grew the sugar and tobacco that made up much of the Atlantic's value; African rulers and merchants controlled supply on the coast.
The African regions that lost most people to the slave trades are the poorest today; raiding broke states and trust and left fragmentation that persists.
note: Feeds a process already under way, so contributed_to rather than caused.

mech: Smallpox, measles, influenza and typhus arriving with Europeans and Africans killed most of the indigenous population within a century.
About 56 million deaths by 1600 let some 56 million hectares of farmland return to forest, drawing down atmospheric CO2 by 7 to 10 ppm and adding to the late-16th and 17th-century cold.
Where soils suited the potato, population and cities grew faster after its adoption; the crop explains about a quarter of Old World population growth from 1700 to 1900.
Sugar, tobacco, tea, coffee and calicoes gave households reasons to sell more labour; women and children spun and wove for the market to buy them.
The Dutch Republic was the first place where households bought most of what they consumed and worked for the market to do so.
Bright, washable Indian cottons were among the new goods that pulled households into longer market work.
Abundant bread, beer and meat from English farms supplied the calories behind long days of heavy work.
Households had already reorganised toward market work and purchased goods, providing the labour and demand the factories later met.
Under the Tokugawa peace, Nobi plain peasants replaced draught animals with family labour and fertiliser, raising output per acre by working harder.
London wages were high relative to capital and very high relative to coal, so it paid to invent machines that swapped capital and coal for labour.
Britain's cotton industry began as an imitation of Indian calicoes, protected by the Calico Acts and pushed by West African demand for Indian-style cloth.
New World land (sugar, cotton, timber) and coal let Britain escape the ecological ceiling that the equally commercial Yangzi delta hit around 1800.
Silver wages in southern England were well above those in the Yangzi delta and India by the 17th and 18th centuries: the gap began before industry.
Mechanisation and steam turned a modest lead into a chasm in output per head.
note: Feeds a process already under way, so contributed_to rather than caused.

mech: Islamic inheritance and partnership law kept firms small and short-lived, and the waqf froze capital, so Middle Eastern merchants never built corporations.
An industrial Enlightenment linked natural philosophers to craftsmen, so useful knowledge flowed into machines.
Portuguese seizures cut Venice's pepper supply after 1502, but by the 1560s Red Sea spice reaching Alexandria was back to its old volumes, much of it under Ottoman protection.
Commodity prices across continents did not converge until the 19th century, so early modern trade was too small and too taxed to transform economies.
